name: Vera Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior designer at Fernhill Studio, a five-person shop above a bike repair place on Canal Street. Most of our clients are theatres, small festivals and charities, so my day is posters, programmes, flyers and the odd logo. I come in at nine, check what Ruth, my art director, marked up overnight in red pen, and spend the morning fixing kerning and moving things around a grid. Honestly, I'm still slow, and she sends a lot back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a poster comes off the big printer and the colours are right, and I can pin it on the wall. I still sketch everything on paper first, which Ruth teases me about. What wears me out is the endless resizing, the same flyer in eleven shapes for different social media sites. And clients who say 'make it pop' and can't tell you what that means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, honestly, and I'd say it loudly on the studio group chat. Everyone's been panicking about AI for two years and I've never touched it. I'd probably post something smug like 'told you so, pencils still work'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, because I'm not a strong designer yet and I know it. If the machines stay mediocre, I get the time I need to get good. My savings mean I'm not scared about money, I'm scared about being found out as slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am and keep asking Ruth to teach me layout properly. I'd take the evening typography course at the art college that I've been putting off, the one that runs on Tuesdays. I'd keep my savings where they are, in the account my grandmother helped me start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of a smug glow, if I'm honest. My job doesn't feel at risk in that picture, only my pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the resizing wears you out. If AI did take that routine part, how would you feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate to admit it, but I'd be glad to lose the resizing. Ruth already says a junior's whole first year is resizing, so maybe I'd get to do real design sooner. I still wouldn't be the one using the tool, though. Felix, the other junior, would do it, and I'd let him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything else on your mind about money or work in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. My partner Tomás is a nurse, his job's steady, and we split the rent on a flat that's cheaper than most. The agency is busy with spring festival work. In a world where nothing changes, I'm doing fine, I just need to get better at my job.

say: I'd say **told you so** on the studio chat, because AI turned out to be hype.
I'd joke that **pencils still work** and the panic was overblown.
think: I'm **relieved**, because I'm a slow junior and need time to improve.
My worry is being **found out as slow**, not money, since my savings are solid.
do: Take the **Tuesday typography course** at the art college this year.
Ask my art director to **teach me layout** properly and keep sketching on paper.
Leave my **savings** untouched in the account my grandmother helped me open.
feel: **Calm**, with a little **smug glow** that my resistance to AI paid off.
S0.quote: If the machines stay mediocre, I get the time I need to get good.
fieldNote: She frames AI as a **test of skill**, not of income, because her cushion is strong.
She'd happily let **another junior** use the tools for resizing rather than learn them herself.
Her partner's **nursing job** makes the household feel steady in this picture.

steps.text: Take the Tuesday evening typography course at the art college
Keep sketching posters by hand and ask Ruth for layout feedback

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say this is what happens when tech companies scrape artists' work without asking. I'd share every post from the designers' guild about copyright and fair pay. At work I'd say we need a proper agreement on how AI gets used, so juniors aren't the first thing cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm exactly the kind of job that goes first. A junior who's slow, doesn't use the tools and costs higher than average pay? If Ruth can get a first draft of a festival flyer from software in ten minutes, why keep me. It makes me feel sick to say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd join the designers' guild properly and pay the dues, which I've been meaning to do. I'd push Ruth to stop hiring freelancers before cutting staff. And I suppose I'd make myself useful on the things software can't do: the press checks at the printer, the hand-lettering, the client meetings. I'd keep my savings as my escape fund rather than spend anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because I've got about nine months of savings and there are lots of studios in the city. But anxious, because the studios won't want juniors either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there are lots of studios nearby. Wouldn't that help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps if they're hiring, but they'd all be doing the same thing as Ruth. Every studio I know is small, and small studios cut the junior first. Having lots of studios nearby just means lots of places to be turned down by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools to keep your place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I really don't want to. It feels like learning to use the machine that stole from my friends who are illustrators. Maybe I'd learn enough to say I know it, but my heart wouldn't be in it, and Ruth would see that.

say: I'd say tech firms **scraped** artists' work and need proper **copyright rules**.
At work I'd ask for an **agreement** so juniors aren't the first cut.
think: I believe a **slow junior** who avoids AI is the first job to go.
My art director could get a **ten-minute draft** from software instead of me.
do: Join the **designers' guild** and pay the dues this spring.
Ask my art director to drop **freelancers before staff** if work shrinks.
Take on **press checks** and hand-lettering, where software can't easily follow.
feel: **Anxious** about being cut, though **nine months** of savings stops it tipping into panic.
S1.quote: Every studio I know is small, and small studios cut the junior first.
fieldNote: She blames **tech companies** and turns to the guild before learning any tools.
Her plenty of local jobs doesn't reassure her, since **every studio** faces the same pressure.
She admits she'd learn AI only **half-heartedly**, and thinks her boss would notice.

steps.text: Join the designers' guild and pay the yearly dues
Ask Ruth to cut freelancers before cutting any staff
Volunteer for press checks and hand-lettering jobs at the studio
Keep nine months of savings untouched as an escape fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments to step in, now, with real support for people losing their work. I'd go on every march about it. Online I'd be one of the angry ones, posting about how the people who built this are getting rich while designers get nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job's over by 2028. Everything I do is on a screen except the sketching and the press checks, and nobody pays a junior just for press checks. The only bit of hope is that the robots come three years later, so hands-on work lasts a little longer. That's the only crack I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the next two years I'd go for something with my hands. I'd ask the screen-printing workshop on Mill Lane if they'd take me on, even part-time, because pulling prints is physical. I'd put a chunk of savings into a proper evening course in sign-painting. And I'd be at the guild meetings and the marches, because this needs a political answer, not just mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It keeps me up just picturing it. I'd be lying awake doing sums about how long the savings last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three extra years before robots mean for you, in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means if I'm pulling screen prints or painting shop signs by 2028, I've got until about 2031 before a robot does that too. Three years isn't a career, it's a breather. But I'd take a breather, and I'd use it to work out what comes next with Tomás.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomás that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm going to be paying less of the rent for a while, and I hate that. He'd say it's fine, because nurses' work is hands-on and people want people. I'd feel like the one who chose the wrong thing at nineteen.

say: I'd say **governments must step in** with real support for people losing work.
Online I'd say AI's **builders get rich** while designers get nothing.
think: I think my screen-based **junior job is over** by 2028.
Robots arriving **three years later** is the only crack of hope I see.
do: Ask the **screen-printing workshop** on Mill Lane for part-time work within months.
Pay for an evening **sign-painting course** out of savings.
Go to **guild meetings and marches** demanding a political answer.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake doing sums on how long **savings last**.
S2.quote: Three years isn't a career, it's a breather.
fieldNote: She sees the robot lag as a **breather**, not a real escape route.
Her move is towards **hands-on craft**, never towards the AI tools.
She feels guilt about **paying less rent** than her partner, a nurse.

steps.text: Ask the Mill Lane screen-printing workshop for part-time work
Pay for an evening sign-painting course from savings
March and attend guild meetings for support for displaced workers
Ask Tomás to cover more of the rent for a while

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like with the fast one, I'd say we need rules and support, but with five years I'd say it more calmly. I'd say it at work, in meetings: let's plan this together, before we're told. I'd post less anger and more organising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd still be around 32 when it hits, with no real design career behind me. That scares me in a different way. I'd have spent five years getting good at something that's then worth nothing, unless I switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself one year to decide, not five. I'd take the screen-printing and sign-painting courses that year, and start doing weekend shifts at the print workshop by year two. I'd keep my studio job meanwhile and save the pay rise I've been promised. And I'd get the guild to push for a retraining fund in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, still. A bit less sharp than the fast one, but I'd still expect to lose the design job. Having time almost makes it worse, because I'd have to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said having time makes it worse. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, the choice is made for me, I just run. Having five years almost makes it worse, because I'd have to look at my boss every Monday knowing I'm planning to leave. Ruth would know something was up. I'm not good at living with a decision hanging over me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the thinking-first, robots-later part? Does that change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the screen goes in 2031 and the hand stuff goes around 2034. So if I'm a printer by 2031, I've maybe got three years more than if I stayed a designer. I'd also want Tomás and me to have the flat sorted by then, so the rent can't swallow us.

say: I'd ask my studio to **plan together** before decisions are made for us.
I'd post **less anger** and more **organising** than in the fast picture.
think: I'd be about **32**, with five years spent on a skill **worth nothing**.
Unless I **switch**, I'd be good at something nobody pays for.
do: Take **screen-printing and sign-painting** courses in the first year.
Start **weekend shifts** at the print workshop by year two.
Save the promised **pay rise** and push the guild for a **retraining fund**.
feel: **Alarmed**, because time forces a **hard choice** she'd rather not face.
S3.quote: Having five years almost makes it worse, because I'd have to look at my boss every Monday knowing I'm planning to leave.
fieldNote: The extra time **adds dread**, because it turns a forced move into her own **decision**.
She plans to be in **hands-on print** before thinking AI lands in 2031.
She wants the **flat settled** with her partner before robots arrive around 2034.

steps.text: Take screen-printing and sign-painting courses next year
Work weekend shifts at the print workshop from year two
Save the whole promised pay rise in the escape fund
Push the guild to lobby the city for a retraining fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd say it's a chance to do this properly. Retraining funds, a shorter working week, designers paid when their work trains AI. I'd say that at guild meetings and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think ten years is enough to get good at a craft that robots reach last. By 2036 I'd be 37 and maybe a decent printer or sign-painter already. The design job still disappears, but I wouldn't be standing there with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Fernhill for maybe three or four years, and actually get good at layout while I learn print on the side. By year five I'd move to the print workshop full-time. I'd put some savings into a share of a small press with two friends from college, if they're up for it. And I'd vote for whoever promises a retraining fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a manageable kind. There's time, and I've got savings, so I feel like I can steer it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd invest in a press. Isn't that a risk for someone who avoids risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I'd hate it. But a press is a real thing in a real room, and I understand it. I'd only put in what I could lose, maybe a third of the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger self, starting the design diploma?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to do the printmaking classes too, not skip them for the computer ones. I'd tell her that the work you do with your hands lasts longer than the work on a screen. She wouldn't listen, though, she wanted to be cool.

say: I'd call ten years **a chance** for retraining funds and a shorter week.
I'd argue designers should be **paid** when their work **trains AI**.
think: I think a decade is enough to master a **craft robots reach last**.
By **37** I'd have a trade, even as the design job disappears.
do: Stay at the studio **three or four years** and learn print on the side.
Move to the **print workshop** full-time around year five.
Put about **a third of savings** into a small press with college friends.
feel: **Anxious** but in a way she can **steer**, thanks to time and savings.
S4.quote: The work you do with your hands lasts longer than the work on a screen.
fieldNote: Even risk-averse, she'd **invest** in a press because she **understands it physically**.
The decade lets her plan a **slow exit** from screen work rather than flight.
She votes and campaigns for **retraining funds**, consistent with her progressive views.

steps.text: Learn print on the side while staying at Fernhill
Move to the print workshop full-time around year five
Put a third of savings into a small press with friends
Vote for candidates who promise a retraining fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. I'd have nothing to show for my design years and very little time to learn a trade. What would help is a paid apprenticeship in printing or sign-making that someone my age could actually get into, not a free online course about using the tools I don't want.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the illustrators I know. They're already losing work now, and they're the reason I won't touch the tools. I'm 27 and I chose a job I thought was safe because it was creative, and creative turned out to be the first thing they automated.

headlineQuote: I chose a job I thought was safe because it was creative, and creative turned out to be the first thing they automated.
portrait: Vera is a **junior designer** at a small studio making theatre and festival posters.
She **never uses AI**, sketches on paper, and blames tech firms for **scraping** artists' work.
Strong **savings** and a partner who's a **nurse** keep money fears lower than skill fears.
Across the scenarios she leans on the **guild** and moves towards **hands-on printing**.
The fast AGI picture **alarms** her most, because it leaves no time to learn a trade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no design career and no time to learn a trade.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** in printing or sign-making open to someone her age, not an AI course.
